abstract: Glutamate/GABA cotransmission allows one neuron to excite and inhibit the same target. How the two release branches translate a shared spike train into net synaptic drive, and how this drive shapes neural circuit activity, remain unclear. We introduce BRIDGE, a model with separate glutamate and GABA resources that deplete and recover under shared input. The model reproduced glutamatergic depression during repeated stimulation in cotransmission recordings. Late GABAergic responses showed weaker frequency dependence. This asymmetry can generate negative differential gain in the model, allowing faster presynaptic firing to weaken net drive while output remains excitatory. In simulated circuits, cotransmitting neurons shifted their output toward excitation when activity fell and toward inhibition when it rose, improving recovery after perturbations across all circuit sizes tested. Compared with baseline, a simplified spiking implementation yielded higher mean accuracy in most classification comparisons and lower error in selected prediction tasks. Thus, resource asymmetry links firing history to bidirectional correction of circuit activity.
